questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I thought it would be interesting to explore a place where not many students from my uni had studied. And the placement of Maastricht geographically in the center or Europe was appealing.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, most things were sent to me from my home university and the exchange university.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: No did not receive any assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I lived in a private accommodation in the first three months, and then switched to the UM Guesthouse for the last 1 1/2 months, due to the fact that my first lease ran out. It was difficult to find off campus housing and it was quite a gamble to know wether you were being scammed or not. But I would recommend joining Facebook groups (just search Maastricht Housing/Rent etc.). I ended up finding my housing through a friend's friend, very randomly.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is expensive renting a room in Maastricht (and all of the Netherlands), so be prepared for a high rent. And be out early! You can always cancel it, but as soon as you know you're going, you should start looking.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You are very much on your own with the housing and the host university or other institutions can't really help you.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I sent my information and nomination from my home university and then they took care of the rest of the process. Signing up for classes was a similar process to the one at KU.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was mainly the Exchange Officer that took care of the process and assisted if there were problems.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes i wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look into the classes and the type of exams assigned to them. It might change slightly each year though.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was about the same as at my home university, however, they required way more during the periods, so you always had to work on something for the course. It was pretty time consuming, and took quite some of your free time.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
They use the PBL (problem based learning) teaching method, but it differed a bit from course to course how much they used it. The idea is basically that the students do all the work in the tutorials, so the teacher is only there for navigating the students in their discussions. Doesn't work too well for exchange students, as we have not tried the method before. However, many times I would be the only exchange student in a class. 
Also the periods of each course were 7-8 weeks, which was a very short time for learning all the material and be ready for the exam, and there was barely any time between the last classes and the exams - sometimes only a couple of days or a weekend.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: European Labour and Social Security Law, Corporate Social Responsibility, European Data Protection and Privacy Law, International Commercial Dispute Resolution, The Good Lawyer

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Good Lawyer is a good and chill course with a take home exam, if you want to have atleast one course that more "exchange friendly". My EU Data Protection course was quite demanding and required a lot of engagement. If you are allowed to, then maybe just take the Data Protection and Privacy course provided on bachelor level for a basic understanding. I felt like I needed a lot of basic/background understanding of several courses, especially in the beginning, so I would reccommend reading up on some stuff before attending. They are also more used to working with EU law than at my home university, so I felt like i lacked a lot of knowledge. Also on private international law, especially regarding common law countries. The two hour written exams were also quite difficult, and many exchange students experienced not passing their courses in the first try.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Needed to buy extra plates, cups etc. when I moved to the Guesthouse because it was badly equipped.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was more expensive and going out to eat, drink and stuff.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Maastricht is a lively city with many opportunities to explore different hobbies etc.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were all sorts of clubs attached to the uni arranging all kinds of activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not participate in a lot of arranged activities, but I went to some ESN (European Student Network) events that were fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Amsterdam, but also Utrecht and Rotterdam. I actually prefer those cities above Amsterdam. Also big student cities.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, it was definitely possible to maintain the same routines as at home, and it was easy to socialize with people as Dutchies are very open!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Focus mainly on socializing with other exchange students, as the ones who are studying here for a longer period of time are more established with their friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really any. Although their food was not really to my liking.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness of the Dutch people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Going to Maastricht University you should be prepared to study a lot and you will most likely be academically challenged - but you would will also learn a lot! Students are in general not Dutch, so no "special treatment" because you're an exchange students, as I've heard others experience elsewhere. The level of english students and teachers speak is generally high, but as everyone is from different countries, you must learn to adapt to the accents.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Spend some time in the beginning to self-study and get some background knowledge for the courses you are taking.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting all the people and getting different inputs from the surroundings and academically.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The courses and the exams.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
